title: Leaky Mitochondria, Stretching Sclera: How mtDAMPs Feed Inflammation in Myopia
content: Background: Myopia is the commonest refractive error worldwide, and progressive axial elongation carries a lifetime risk of pathologic myopia with irreversible posterior-segment damage. Alongside abnormal retinal signalling, choroidal thinning and scleral remodelling, myopic eyes show a low-grade inflammatory and redox disturbance, yet the events that sustain it remain unsettled. Mitochondria sit at the junction of energy supply, redox control, calcium handling and innate immune signalling, and stressed mitochondria release mitochondrial damage-associated molecular patterns (mtDAMPs) such as mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), reactive oxygen species (ROS), ATP and cardiolipin. Whether mitochondrial dysfunction drives the inflammatory component of myopia, and in which cell type, is unresolved. Main body: We follow the evidence along one retinal–choroidal–scleral axis and consider three compartments separately: retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, Müller glia and scleral fibroblasts. For each compartment we separate direct myopia data from mechanistic inference drawn from photo-oxidative, hypoxic or inflammatory injury models, and grade the evidence rather than treating all observations as equivalent. The strongest disease-specific evidence concerns scleral fibroblasts, where hypoxia and mechanical strain intersect with mitochondrial metabolism and dynamics, and where inflammasome activation, IL-1β/IL-6 signalling and MMP-2-dependent matrix loss converge on fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition; DRP1-dependent fission, NAT2 and respiratory-chain genes including COX3, ND2 and ND4 have been examined in myopic tissue and scleral cell models. Evidence in RPE cells is moderate for an inflammatory contribution but weak for a mitochondrial upstream mechanism, whereas Müller glia provide a plausible relay whose mitochondrial involvement remains largely inferred. We also consider how hormonal and circadian inputs and ageing modify this axis, and summarise candidate interventions with their level of evidence. Conclusion: Mitochondrial stress is a credible but not yet demonstrated driver of myopic inflammation. The axis described here is best regarded as a testable model rather than a demonstrated linear pathway; the decisive experiments must establish temporal order by measuring mitochondrial respiration, mtROS, cytosolic mtDNA, cGAMP, STING/TBK1 phosphorylation, NLRP3 activation and ECM biomechanics before and during axial elongation.
